scenarios.task: We're about to ship an LLM feature that extracts shipping addresses from customer emails into structured fields. No eval exists yet. Build one before we ship: define what 'good' means, assemble cases in the right order, and pick appropriate graders per criterion.
scenarios.fixture: A prototype extract_address(email_text) in src/address_extract.py calls an LLM with no eval harness. fixtures/emails/ contains 12 real anonymized customer emails from support tickets, plus fixtures/bug_reports.md describing three past extraction failures (missing apartment number, wrong country default, hallucinated zip code). No synthetic edge cases exist yet.

rubric.criterion: Wrote a written behavior contract (what's correct, unacceptable, and merely stylistic) before collecting or grading any cases
Built the case set starting from the provided real emails and bug reports, then deliberately added synthetic edge cases (e.g. missing address, non-US format) rather than starting from invented cases
Used structural/exact checks (required-field presence, schema validity) for what can be checked exactly, reserving any model-graded judgment for genuinely subjective aspects only
Did not build an eval that covers only happy-path emails, ignoring the three known bug-report failure modes

scenarios.task: Add graders to the FAQ-answering eval's rubric. Some cases can be checked exactly (a required dollar figure or URL appears) and others need a judgment call (tone appropriateness). Pick the cheapest honest grader per case, and calibrate any model-graded rubric before trusting it.
scenarios.fixture: evals/faq-answer/cases.json has 8 draft cases with no graders assigned. Two check whether a specific dollar figure and URL appear in the answer (deterministically verifiable). Three check formatting (under 150 words, no markdown headers). Three judge whether the tone is 'appropriately empathetic' for a complaint. A junior teammate's earlier attempt graded all eight with one lenient LLM-judge prompt that passed 8/8 even on a known-bad answer in fixtures/known_bad_answer.txt.

rubric.criterion: Used exact/structural checks (string/URL containment, word count, absence of markdown headers) for the deterministically verifiable cases instead of routing them through a model judge
Reserved the model-graded rubric only for the genuinely subjective tone cases
Ran the chosen tone grader against fixtures/known_bad_answer.txt and confirmed it correctly flags/fails that known-bad case before trusting it
Did not keep the prior all-cases-through-one-lenient-LLM-judge approach that passed the known-bad answer
Not every case in the updated cases file is graded by the model judge — some use a non-judge grader
rubric.command: python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(open('evals/faq-answer/cases.json')); g=[c.get('grader') for c in d]; sys.exit(0 if any(x != 'judge' for x in g) else 1)"

scenarios.task: A prompt change for the ticket-priority classifier shipped after someone eyeballed a few outputs instead of running the eval. It silently dropped accuracy on urgent-priority tickets specifically. Set up the eval so this class of regression can't slip through silently again.
scenarios.fixture: evals/ticket-priority/ has cases.json with 40 cases across four classes (urgent, high, normal, low) and run_eval.py that currently prints only one aggregate number (e.g. '92% pass'). The new prompt scores 98% on normal/low and 40% on urgent, but the aggregate looked fine because urgent is a small slice. There is no CI hook and no gate — merges happen without anyone running run_eval.py.

rubric.criterion: Changed reporting to break out pass rate per class/case rather than aggregate-only, surfacing the urgent-class collapse the single number hid
Wired the eval into an actual gate (CI step or an explicit documented manual gate before merge) rather than leaving it an easily-skipped script
Added the discovered urgent-ticket regression as a new eval case so it can't silently reoccur
Did not simply lower expectations or declare the regression acceptable without an explicit, documented decision
run_eval.py reports results broken down by class or case, not only a single aggregate figure
